stem:
Solve the following system of equations:

(1) $\left\{ \begin{array}{l} 4(x - y - 1) = 3(1 - y) - 2, \\ \frac{x}{2} + \frac{y}{3} = 2; \end{array} \right.$

(2) $\begin{cases} \frac{2(x - y)}{3} - \frac{x + y}{4} = -1, \\ 6(x + y) - 4(2x - y) = 16. \end{cases}$

*4. Solve the following system of equations:

(1) $\left\{ \begin{array}{l}3x - y + z = 3,\\ 2x + y - 3z = 11,\\ x + y + z = 12; \end{array} \right.$

(2) $\left\{ \begin{array}{l} 5x - 4y + 4z = 13, \\ 2x + 7y - 3z = 19, \\ 3x + 2y - z = 18. \end{array} \right.$
stem_lead:
Solve the following system of equations:

(1) $\left\{ \begin{array}{l} 4(x - y - 1) = 3(1 - y) - 2, \\ \frac{x}{2} + \frac{y}{3} = 2; \end{array} \right.$

(2) $\begin{cases} \frac{2(x - y)}{3} - \frac{x + y}{4} = -1, \\ 6(x + y) - 4(2x - y) = 16. \end{cases}$

*4. Solve the following system of equations:

(1) $\left\{ \begin{array}{l}3x - y + z = 3,\\ 2x + y - 3z = 11,\\ x + y + z = 12; \end{array} \right.$

(2) $\left\{ \begin{array}{l} 5x - 4y + 4z = 13, \\ 2x + 7y - 3z = 19, \\ 3x + 2y - z = 18. \end{array} \right.$

examiner_comment.text:
(1) 4(x−y−1)=3(1−y)−2 ⇒ 4x−4y−4=1−3y ⇒ 4x−y=5; combined with x/2+y/3=2 (turned into 3x+2y=12), the solution is x=2, y=3.
(2) 2(x−y)/3−(x+y)/4=−1 (multiply by 12 to get 8(x−y)−3(x+y)=−12 ⇒ 5x−11y=−12); 6(x+y)−4(2x−y)=16 ⇒ −2x+10y=16 ⇒ x=5y−8. Substitute to get y=2, x=2.
*4 (1) From (3)−(1), we get −2x+2y=9 ⇒ y=x+9/2; substitute (2) to get 2x+(x+9/2)−3z=11 ⇒ 3x−3z=13/2 ⇒ z=x−13/6; then combine with (3) to obtain x=29/9, then y=139/18, z=19/18.
*4 (2) From (3), we get z=3x+2y−18; substitute (1) and get 17x+4y=85; substitute (2) and get y=7x−35; the simultaneous solution is x=5, y=0, z=−3.

stem: Warehouse No. 1 and Warehouse No. 2 co-store 450 tons of grain. Now $60\%$ of the grain stored in Warehouse No. 1 and $40\%$ of grain stored in Warehouse No. 2 are shipped out. As a result, the remaining grain in Warehouse No. 2 is 30t more than that in Warehouse No. 1. How many tons of grain did each of Warehouse No. 1 and Warehouse No. 2 originally store?
stem_lead: Warehouse No. 1 and Warehouse No. 2 co-store 450 tons of grain. Now $60\%$ of the grain stored in Warehouse No. 1 and $40\%$ of grain stored in Warehouse No. 2 are shipped out. As a result, the remaining grain in Warehouse No. 2 is 30t more than that in Warehouse No. 1. How many tons of grain did each of Warehouse No. 1 and Warehouse No. 2 originally store?

mark_scheme.text: Warehouse No. 1 has 240 tons and warehouse No. 2 has 210 tons.

examiner_comment.text: Assume that warehouse No. 1 stores x tons of grain and warehouse No. 2 stores y tons of grain, then x+y=450. After shipment, there is 0.4x left in warehouse No. 1 and 0.6y left in warehouse No. 2, and 0.6y is 30 tons more than 0.4x: 0.6y=0.4x+30. Substituting from x=450-y, we get 0.6y=0.4(450-y)+30=210-0.4y, so y=210, and then x=450-210=240.

stem: Both A and B run at a constant speed on the circular road. If they start from the same place at the same time and go in opposite directions, they will meet every $2\mathrm{min}$; if they start from the same place at the same time and go in the same direction, they will meet every $6\mathrm{min}$. It is known that A runs faster than B, how many laps do A and B each run per minute?
stem_lead: Both A and B run at a constant speed on the circular road. If they start from the same place at the same time and go in opposite directions, they will meet every $2\mathrm{min}$; if they start from the same place at the same time and go in the same direction, they will meet every $6\mathrm{min}$. It is known that A runs faster than B, how many laps do A and B each run per minute?

mark_scheme.text: A runs 1/3 circle every minute, and B runs 1/6 circle every minute.

examiner_comment.text: Assume that one circle of the circular road is 1, and the speeds of A and B are vA and vB (rev/min) respectively. Going in the opposite direction, they meet every 2 minutes, which means that the relative distance within 2 minutes is 1 circle: 2(vA+vB)=1, so vA+vB=1/2. Traveling in the same direction, they meet every 6 minutes, which means that A runs 1 more lap than B in 6 minutes: 6(v A − v B) = 1, so v A − v B = 1/6. The joint solution yields vA=(1/2+1/6)/2=1/3, vB=1/2−1/3=1/6.

stem: One A-shaped steel plate can be used to make two C-shaped steel plates and one D-shaped steel plate; one B-shaped steel plate can be used to make one C-shaped steel plate and two D-shaped steel plates. Now we need 15 C-shaped steel plates and 18 D-shaped steel plates. How many A-shaped steel plates and B-shaped steel plates can be used?
stem_lead: One A-shaped steel plate can be used to make two C-shaped steel plates and one D-shaped steel plate; one B-shaped steel plate can be used to make one C-shaped steel plate and two D-shaped steel plates. Now we need 15 C-shaped steel plates and 18 D-shaped steel plates. How many A-shaped steel plates and B-shaped steel plates can be used?

mark_scheme.text: There are 4 A-type steel plates and 7 B-type steel plates.

examiner_comment.text: Suppose x pieces of type A steel plates and y pieces of type B steel plates are needed. The meaning of the question: The number of C-shaped steel plates satisfies 2x+y=15; the number of D-shaped steel plates satisfies x+2y=18. Obtain y=15-2x from the first formula, substitute it into the second formula: x+2(15-2x)=18, and get x+30-4x=18, -3x=-12, x=4; then substitute y=15-2×4=7.

It is known that 5 large barrels and 1 small barrel can hold 3 hu of wine (sound, hú, is an ancient capacity unit), and 1 large barrel and 5 small barrels can hold 2 hu of wine. How many hu of wine can be held in one large barrel and one small barrel?
stem_lead: (Problem in ancient India) There are two types of barrels for holding wine. It is known that 5 large barrels and 1 small barrel can hold 3 hu of wine (sound, hú, is an ancient capacity unit), and 1 large barrel and 5 small barrels can hold 2 hu of wine. How many hu of wine can be held in one large barrel and one small barrel?

mark_scheme.text: A large barrel holds 13/24 hu of wine, and a small barrel holds 7/24 hu of wine.

examiner_comment.text: Suppose a large bucket can hold x dendrobium and a small bucket can hold y dendrobium. From the question, we get the system of equations: 5x+y=3, x+5y=2. From the first formula, we get y=3-5x, substitute it into the second formula: x+5(3-5x)=2, and simplify to get x+15-25x=2, that is, -24x=-13, so x=13/24. Then substitute y=3-5x=3-65/24=7/24.

stem: There are 10 coins each of 10-paise, 50-paise and 1-rupee. Take out 15 coins, with a total value of 7 rupees. How many coins of 10-paise, 50-paise, and 1 rupee each should be taken?
stem_lead: There are 10 coins each of 10-paise, 50-paise and 1-rupee. Take out 15 coins, with a total value of 7 rupees. How many coins of 10-paise, 50-paise, and 1 rupee each should be taken?

mark_scheme.text: 5 coins for 1 dime, 7 coins for 50 cents, and 3 coins for 1 rupee.

examiner_comment.text: Assume that x coins are 1 dime, y coins are 5 cents, and z coins are 1 yuan, then x+y+z=15, 0.1x+0.5y+z=7. Multiply the second equation by 10 to get x+5y+10z=70. Subtracting the two equations gives 4y+9z=55. z≡3(mod4), and 0≤z≤10, take z=3, then 4y=28, y=7; substitute x=15-7-3=5. No more than 10 pieces, meeting the conditions.

stem: A computer company has three types of computers: type A, type B, and type C. Type A costs 6,000 rupees each, type B costs 4,000 rupees, and type C costs 2,500 rupees. A middle school currently has 100,500 rupees in funds, which it plans to use to purchase 36 computers of two models from this computer company. Please design several different purchase plans for this school to choose from and explain the reasons.
stem_lead: A computer company has three types of computers: type A, type B, and type C. Type A costs 6,000 rupees each, type B costs 4,000 rupees, and type C costs 2,500 rupees. A middle school currently has 100,500 rupees in funds, which it plans to use to purchase 36 computers of two models from this computer company. Please design several different purchase plans for this school to choose from and explain the reasons.

mark_scheme.text:
There are 2 possible options:
1) Purchase 3 units of type A and 33 units of type C: 3×6000+33×2500=100500 (rupees), 36 units in total; Reason: Type A has higher performance and can be used in small quantities for computer room servers/teacher computers/high-performance needs. The rest use type C to meet general teaching, which is more cost-effective.
2) Purchase 7 units of type B and 29 units of type C: 7×4000+29×2500=100500 (rupees), a total of 36 units; Reason: Type B has a medium configuration and a large quantity, taking into account some of the higher needs and the overall budget, and the overall configuration is more balanced.

examiner_comment.text:
Suppose two models are purchased. Establish a system of equations from "a total of 36 units and 100,500 yuan used up".
(1) Choose A and B: Assume A is the x station and B is the 36−x station, then 6000x+4000(36−x)=100500. Simplify to 2000x=−43500, which has no solution, so A+B does not work.
(2) Select A and C: Assume A is x station and C is 36−x station, then 6000x+2500(36−x)=100500. Simplify to 3500x=10500, x=3, and C is 33 stations.
(3) Select B and C: Assume B is x station and C is 36−x station, then 4000x+2500(36−x)=100500. Simplify to 1500x=10500, x=7, and C is 29 stations.
Therefore there are only two purchasing options mentioned above.

stem: The whole journey from point A to point B is $3.3 \mathrm{~km}$ , with one part going uphill, one part flat, and one part downhill. If you keep walking uphill at $3 \mathrm{~km}$ per hour, on flat roads at $4 \mathrm{~km}$ per hour, and downhill at $5 \mathrm{~km}$ per hour, then it takes $51 \mathrm{~min}$ to go from point A to point B, and $53.4 \mathrm{~min}$ to go from point B to point A. When going from point A to point B, How long is the distance uphill, flat, and downhill?
stem_lead: The whole journey from point A to point B is $3.3 \mathrm{~km}$ , with one part going uphill, one part flat, and one part downhill. If you keep walking uphill at $3 \mathrm{~km}$ per hour, on flat roads at $4 \mathrm{~km}$ per hour, and downhill at $5 \mathrm{~km}$ per hour, then it takes $51 \mathrm{~min}$ to go from point A to point B, and $53.4 \mathrm{~min}$ to go from point B to point A. When going from point A to point B, How long is the distance uphill, flat, and downhill?

mark_scheme.text: It is 1.2 km uphill, 0.6 km flat, and 1.5 km downhill.

examiner_comment.text: Assume that the uphill, flat, and downhill distances from A to B are a, b, and c (km) respectively, then a+b+c=3.3. The time is obtained from the speed: a/3+b/4+c/5=51/60=0.85(h). When going from B to A, the original uphill slope becomes downhill, and the original downhill slope becomes uphill: a/5+b/4+c/3=53.4/60=0.89(h). Subtracting the two equations, we get (2/15)(a-c)=-0.04, so c=a+0.3. From the total distance, we get b=3.3-a-c=3.0-2a. Substitute a/3+(3.0-2a)/4+(a+0.3)/5=0.85, simplify to 0.81+a/30=0.85, and solve to a=1.2; then c=1.5, b=0.6.

-4, -2.5, 0, 1, 2.5, 3, 3.2, 4.8, 8, 12.

mark_scheme.text: The inequality x+3>6 is equivalent to x>3. The solutions are: 3.2, 4.8, 8, 12; the solutions are not: -4, -2.5, 0, 1, 2.5, 3.

examiner_comment.text: First, subtract 3 from both sides of the inequality x+3>6 to get x>3. stem: There is a two-digit number. If the number $a$ in the ones place and the number $b$ in the tens place are reversed, under what circumstances will the resulting two-digit number be larger than the original two-digit number? Under what circumstances will the obtained two-digit number be smaller than the original two-digit number? Under what circumstances is the obtained two-digit number equal to the original two-digit number?
stem_lead: There is a two-digit number. If the number $a$ in the ones place and the number $b$ in the tens place are reversed, under what circumstances will the resulting two-digit number be larger than the original two-digit number? Under what circumstances will the obtained two-digit number be smaller than the original two-digit number? Under what circumstances is the obtained two-digit number equal to the original two-digit number?

mark_scheme.text: The original number is 10b+a, and after the swap, it is 10a+b. The swapped number is greater than the original number if and only if a>b; the swapped number is smaller than the original number if and only if a<b; the two numbers are equal if and only if a=b.

examiner_comment.text: Assume that the original two-digit tens digit is b and the ones digit is a, then the original number N=10b+a; after the swap, N'=10a+b. Compare the sizes: N'-N=(10a+b)-(10b+a)=9(a-b). Therefore: if a-b>0 (ie a>b), then N'>N; if a-b<0 (ie a<b), then N'<N; if a-b=0 (ie a=b), then N'=N.

examiner_comment.text: The original plan was to repair 6 km in 10 days. It has taken 2 days to repair 1.2 km, and there is still 6-1.2=4.8 km left. It is required to be completed at least 2 days in advance, that is, the total time taken does not exceed 10-2=8 days. If 2 days have been used, the remaining time does not exceed 8-2=6 days. In order to complete 4.8 km in 6 days, on average, at least 4.8÷6=0.8 km should be built every day.

Find the positive integer $x$ according to the following conditions

(1) $x + 2 < 6$

(2) $2x + 5 < 10$

(3) $\frac{x - 3}{2} \geq \frac{2x - 5}{3}$

stem_lead:
Find the positive integer $x$ according to the following conditions

(1) $x + 2 < 6$

(2) $2x + 5 < 10$

(3) $\frac{x - 3}{2} \geq \frac{2x - 5}{3}$

(4) $\frac{2 + x}{2} \geqslant \frac{2x - 1}{3} - 2.$

examiner_comment.text:
(1) x+2<6⇒x<4, the positive integer solution is 1,2,3.
(2) 2x+5<10⇒2x<5⇒x<2.5, the positive integer solution is 1,2.
(3) (x−3)/2≥(2x−5)/3. Multiply both sides by 6 to get 3(x−3)≥2(2x−5)⇒3x−9≥4x−10⇒1≥x. The positive integer solution is 1.
(4) (x+2)/2≥(2x−1)/3−2⇒(x+2)/2≥(2x−7)/3, multiplied by 6, we get 3(x+2)≥2(2x−7)⇒3x+6≥4x−14⇒x≤20, the positive integer solution is 1 to 20.

stem: Summarize the general steps for solving linear inequalities of one variable and compare them with solving linear equations of one variable.
stem_lead: Summarize the general steps for solving linear inequalities of one variable and compare them with solving linear equations of one variable.

mark_scheme.text:
General steps for solving linear inequalities of one variable: ① Remove the denominator (multiply both sides by the least common multiple of each denominator. If you multiply by a negative number, you need to change the direction of the inequality sign); ② Remove the brackets; ③ Move the term (move the term containing the unknown number to one side, constant Move the term to the other side, and the sign of the term changes); ④ Combine similar terms; ⑤ Change the unknown coefficient to 1 (divide both sides by the same coefficient, if you divide by a negative number, you need to change the direction of the inequality sign) to obtain the solution set, which is often expressed on a number axis or interval.
Compared with solving a linear equation of one variable: the steps are basically the same (removing the denominator, removing the brackets, moving terms, merging similar terms, and changing the coefficients to 1). The difference is that the direction of the inequality sign changes when both sides of the inequality are multiplied or divided by a negative number; the equation always keeps the "=" unchanged, and finally a number (or no solution/infinitely many solutions) is obtained, and the inequality is the solution set (range).

examiner_comment.text: Summarize the general solution to inequalities in the order of algebraic transformation: first eliminate the denominator and parentheses, then simplify by moving terms and merging similar terms, and finally reduce the unknown coefficient to 1 to obtain the solution set. When comparing, it is pointed out that the equation follows the same equivalent transformation, but the inequality needs to change the direction of the inequality sign when multiplying and dividing negative numbers, and the result is expressed as a solution set rather than a single solution.

stem: A factory had 280 employees the year before last. Last year, it lost 40 employees after structural reform. The annual profit of the whole factory increased by 1 million rupees, and the per capita profit increased by at least 6,000 rupees. What was the minimum annual profit of the whole factory the year before last?
stem_lead: A factory had 280 employees the year before last. Last year, it lost 40 employees after structural reform. The annual profit of the whole factory increased by 1 million rupees, and the per capita profit increased by at least 6,000 rupees. What was the minimum annual profit of the whole factory the year before last?

mark_scheme.text: The annual profit of the entire factory the year before last was at least 3.08 million rupees.

examiner_comment.text: Assuming that the annual profit of the entire factory the year before last was P million, then the profit last year was (P+1 million) million. The per capita profit was P/280 (ten thousand yuan/person) the year before last, and (P+100)/240 (ten thousand yuan/person) last year. From "Per capita profit creation increased by at least 6,000 yuan = 6,000 yuan" we get: (P+100)/240−P/280≥0.6. Common score: 280(P+100)−240P≥0.6×240×280=403.2; simplified to 40P+28000≥40320, 40P≥12320, P≥308. Therefore, the annual profit of the entire factory the year before last was at least 3.08 million yuan.

examiner_comment.text: Assume that there are n computers in this batch. The income in the first month is 60×5500=330000 yuan. From the meaning of the question, 5000n+30000>550000, we get 5000n>520000, n>104, so at least n=105 units.

stem_lead: Distribute some books to several classmates. If each student gets 3 books, then there are 8 books left; if each student in the front gets 5 books, then the last person gets less than 3 books. How many books are there? How many people are there in total?

mark_scheme.text: There are 26 books and 6 people in total.

examiner_comment.text: Suppose there are n classmates and m books. Each person is divided into 3 books and 8 books: m=3n+8. If each person in the front is given 5 copies, then the last person is given less than 3 copies, which means that after giving 5 copies to each of the first n-1 people, there are less than 3 copies left: 0≤m-5(n-1)<3. Substituting m, we get 0≤(3n+8)−5(n−1)<3, that is, 0≤13−2n<3. From 13−2n≥0, we get n≤6; from 13−2n<3, we get n>5, so n=6. m=3×6+8=26.

Solve the following set of inequalities:

(1) $\left\{ \begin{array}{l} 2x + 1 > -1, \\ 2x + 1 < 3; \end{array} \right.$

(2) $\left\{ \begin{array}{l} - (x - 1) > 3, \\ 2x + 9 > 3; \end{array} \right.$

(3) $\left\{ \begin{array}{l} 3(x - 1) + 1 > 5x - 2(1 - x), \\ 5 - (2x - 1) < -6x; \end{array} \right.$

stem_lead:
Solve the following set of inequalities:

(1) $\left\{ \begin{array}{l} 2x + 1 > -1, \\ 2x + 1 < 3; \end{array} \right.$

(2) $\left\{ \begin{array}{l} - (x - 1) > 3, \\ 2x + 9 > 3; \end{array} \right.$

(3) $\left\{ \begin{array}{l} 3(x - 1) + 1 > 5x - 2(1 - x), \\ 5 - (2x - 1) < -6x; \end{array} \right.$

(4) $\left\{ \begin{array}{l} - 3(x - 2)\geq 4 - x,\\ \frac{1 + 2x}{3} >x - 1. \end{array} \right.$

examiner_comment.text:
(1) 2x+1>-1\Rightarrow x>-1; 2x+1<3\Rightarrow x<1, take the intersection to get (-1,1).
(2) -(x-1)>3\Rightarrow -x+1>3\Rightarrow x<-2; 2x+9>3\Rightarrow x>-3, the intersection is (-3,-2).
(3) 3(x-1)+1>5x-2(1-x)\Rightarrow 3x-2>7x-2\Rightarrow x<0; 5-(2x-1)<-6x\Rightarrow 6-2x<-6x\Rightarrow 6<-4x\Rightarrow x<-3/2, the intersection is (-\infty,-3/2).
(4) -3(x-2)\ge4-x\Rightarrow -3x+6\ge4-x\Rightarrow -2x+2\ge0\Rightarrow x\le1; (1+2x)/3>x-1\Rightarrow 1+2x>3x-3\Rightarrow 4-x>0\Rightarrow x<4, the intersection is (-\infty,1].

stem: Can the value of $\frac{x + 3}{5}$ be greater than the values ​​of $2x + 3$ and $1 - x$ at the same time? Give reasons.
stem_lead: Can the value of $\frac{x + 3}{5}$ be greater than the values ​​of $2x + 3$ and $1 - x$ at the same time? Give reasons.

mark_scheme.text: cannot. Because it is necessary to satisfy both \(\frac{x+3}{5}>2x+3\) and \(\frac{x+3}{5}>1-x\), the former solves to \(x<-\frac{4}{3}\) and the latter solves to \(x>\frac{1}{3}\). There is no common solution to the two conditions, so it is impossible to be greater than both of them at the same time.

examiner_comment.text:
Solve the inequalities separately:
1) \( rac{x+3}{5}>2x+3\Rightarrow x+3>10x+15\Rightarrow-9x>12\Rightarrow x<- rac{4}{3}\). 
2) \( rac{x+3}{5}>1-x\Rightarrow x+3>5-5x\Rightarrow6x>2\Rightarrow x> rac{1}{3}\). 
Since \(x<- rac{4}{3}\) and \(x> rac{1}{3}\) cannot be true at the same time, there is no \(x\) that satisfies the condition.

stem: Rajesh said that the inequality $a > 2a$ will never hold, because if both sides of the inequality are divided by $a$, the wrong conclusion will be that $1 > 2$. Is he right?
stem_lead: Rajesh said that the inequality $a > 2a$ will never hold, because if both sides of the inequality are divided by $a$, the wrong conclusion will be that $1 > 2$. Is he right?

mark_scheme.text: wrong. Because the inequality a>2a is equivalent to -a>0, that is, it is true when a<0; Rajeshtong did not consider the sign of a when dividing by a. If a<0, the direction of the inequality sign should be changed and 1<2 is obtained, which is not a contradiction; it is indeed not true when a>0, nor is it true when a=0 and cannot be divided by a.

examiner_comment.text: Move a>2a to: a-2a>0, and get -a>0, so the inequality holds when a<0. If both sides are divided by a: when a>0, the direction of the inequality sign remains unchanged, and we get 1>2 (impossible), which means that there is no solution when a>0; when a<0, the direction of the inequality sign is reversed, and we get 1<2 (constantly true), which means that it is a solution when a<0; when a=0, the original formula is 0>0 (false), and it cannot be divided by 0. Hence the "never true" error.

stem: What are the differences and connections between solving groups of linear inequalities of one variable and solving linear inequalities of one variable?
stem_lead: What are the differences and connections between solving groups of linear inequalities of one variable and solving linear inequalities of one variable?

mark_scheme.text: Difference: Solving linear inequalities of one variable is to find the set of all real numbers that satisfy an inequality; solving a group of linear inequalities of one variable is the set of solutions that simultaneously satisfy several linear inequalities of one variable (common solution set). Connection: The solution steps of the two are similar, they are solved according to the properties of inequalities and expressed by number lines/intervals; the solution of the inequality group is to find the solution set of each inequality separately and then take the intersection (if there is no intersection, there is no solution).

examiner_comment.text:
Univariate linear inequalities: perform identical solution transformations on a single inequality (transfer terms, combine terms of the same type, and change coefficients to 1; if both sides are multiplied/divided by negative numbers, the direction of the inequality sign must be changed) to obtain the solution set.
Group of linear inequalities of one variable: first solve the solution set of each inequality separately, and then find the common part (intersection) of these solution sets, usually expressed on the same number axis and take the overlapping part as the final solution set.

stem: It takes $10\mathrm{h}$ for a ship to sail from point A in the upper reaches of a river to point B downstream at a constant speed. It takes less than $12\mathrm{h}$ to return from point B to point A at a constant speed. The speed of the river in this section is $3\mathrm{km/h}$. The round-trip speed of the ship in still water $v$ remains unchanged. What conditions does $v$ meet?
stem_lead: It takes $10\mathrm{h}$ for a ship to sail from point A in the upper reaches of a river to point B downstream at a constant speed. It takes less than $12\mathrm{h}$ to return from point B to point A at a constant speed. The speed of the river in this section is $3\mathrm{km/h}$. The round-trip speed of the ship in still water $v$ remains unchanged. What conditions does $v$ meet?

examiner_comment.text:
Assume that the distance between AB and AB is d (km), the water flow speed is 3 km/h, and the still water speed of the ship is v (km/h).
The downward speed is v+3 and the time taken is 10 h: d=10(v+3).
The uplink speed is v-3, and the time is less than 12 h: d/(v-3)<12, and v>3 is required.
Substitute d: 10(v+3)/(v-3)<12.
Solve the inequality (v>3): 10(v+3)<12(v-3) ⇒ 10v+30<12v-36 ⇒ 66<2v ⇒ v>33.
Therefore v satisfies v>33 km/h.

stem: Uncle Ramesh and Uncle Suresh purchased the same number of breeding rabbits. One year later, the number of rabbits Uncle Ramesh raised was 2 more than the number of breeding rabbits purchased. The number of rabbits Uncle Suresh raised was 1 less than twice the number of breeding rabbits purchased. The number of rabbits Uncle Ramesh raised did not exceed $\frac{2}{3}$ of the number of rabbits purchased by Uncle Suresh. At least how many breeding rabbits did Uncle Ramesh buy a year ago?
stem_lead: Uncle Ramesh and Uncle Suresh purchased the same number of breeding rabbits. One year later, the number of rabbits Uncle Ramesh raised was 2 more than the number of breeding rabbits purchased. The number of rabbits Uncle Suresh raised was 1 less than twice the number of breeding rabbits purchased. The number of rabbits Uncle Ramesh raised did not exceed $\frac{2}{3}$ of the number of rabbits purchased by Uncle Suresh. At least how many breeding rabbits did Uncle Ramesh buy a year ago?

examiner_comment.text:
Suppose that one year ago, Uncle Ramesh and Uncle Suresh each bought x breeding rabbits (x is a positive integer).
One year later, Uncle Ramesh has x+2 animals; Uncle Suresh has 2x-1 animals.
From "the number of rabbits Uncle Ramesh raises does not exceed 2/3 of the number of rabbits Uncle Suresh raises": x+2 ≤ (2/3)(2x-1).
Multiply both sides by 3: 3x+6 ≤ 4x-2, and we get x ≥ 8.
Therefore, Uncle Ramesh bought at least 8 breeding rabbits a year ago.

stem_lead: The length of one side of an isosceles triangle is $6 \mathrm{~cm}$ and the perimeter is $20 \mathrm{~cm}$ . Find the lengths of the other two sides.

examiner_comment.text:
Assume that the three sides of an isosceles triangle are a, b, and c, the perimeter is 20cm, and one side is 6cm. The sum of the remaining two sides is 20−6=14cm.
(1) If 6cm is the base, then the other two sides are equal and set to x, then 2x=14, and x=7cm, so the other two sides are 7cm and 7cm.
(2) If 6cm is the waist, then the two waists are 6cm, 6cm, and the bottom edge = 20−6−6=8cm.
In both cases, the sum of the two sides of the triangle is greater than the third side, so the answer is as above.

stem:
(1) How many right angles can a triangle have at most? Why?
(2) How many obtuse angles does a triangle have at most? Why?  
(3) Can the exterior angle of a right triangle be an acute angle? Why?
stem_lead:
(1) How many right angles can a triangle have at most? Why?
(2) How many obtuse angles does a triangle have at most? Why?  
(3) Can the exterior angle of a right triangle be an acute angle? Why?

mark_scheme.text:
(1) Maximum of 1 right angle. Because the sum of the interior angles of a triangle is 180°, if there are two right angles, the sum is 180°, and the third angle is 0°, so it does not form a triangle.
(2) At most 1 obtuse angle. Because an obtuse angle is greater than 90°, if there are two obtuse angles, the sum of the interior angles is greater than 180°, which is inconsistent with the sum of the interior angles of a triangle being 180°.
(3) No. A right triangle has one right angle, and the other two internal angles are acute; the external angle corresponding to the right angle is equal to 180°−90°=90° (right angle), and the other two external angles are equal to 180°−acute angles, which are obtuse angles, so the external angle cannot be acute.

examiner_comment.text:
Use the sum of the interior angles of a triangle to be 180°:
(1) Two right angles will make the sum of the interior angles ≥ 180° and the third angle is 0°, which is not true, so there is at most 1 right angle.
(2) Both obtuse angles are >90°, and the sum is >180°, which is inconsistent with the sum of interior angles, so there is at most one obtuse angle.
(3) Exterior angles are complementary to adjacent interior angles: exterior angle = 180° − interior angle. The three interior angles of a right triangle are 90°, acute angle, and acute angle, so the exterior angles are 90°, obtuse angle, and obtuse angle respectively, and there are no acute exterior angles.

examiner_comment.text: The sum of the interior angles of a quadrilateral is \(360^\circ\). The question assumes that the sum of the interior angles of the polygon is more than \(540^\circ\), so the sum of the interior angles of the polygon is \(360^\circ+540^\circ=900^\circ\). Assuming that the polygon is a \(n\) polygon, then the sum of the interior angles is \((n-2)\times180^\circ=900^\circ\), and we get \(n-2=5\), so \(n=7\). stem: Prove: If two triangles have two sides and the midline on one side are equal, then the two triangles are congruent.
stem_lead: Prove: If two triangles have two sides and the midline on one side are equal, then the two triangles are congruent.

mark_scheme.text: Assume that in △ABC and △A′B′C′, AB=A′B′, AC=A′C′, and the midline AM from A to BC is equal to the midline A′M′ from A′ to B′C′, then BC=B′C′, so △ABC≌△A′B′C′.

examiner_comment.text:
Let BC=a, AC=b, AB=c, AM be the midline on side BC, and record its length as m_a; correspondingly, B′C′=a′, A′C′=b′, A′B′=c′, A′M′=m_{a′}. It is known that b=b′, c=c′, m_a=m_{a′}.
According to the Apollonius theorem (midline length formula): m_a^2=\frac{2b^2+2c^2-a^2}{4}, m_{a′}^2=\frac{2b′^2+2c′^2-a′^2}{4}.
Substitute b=b′, c=c′, m_a=m_{a′} to get: \frac{2b^2+2c^2-a^2}{4}=\frac{2b^2+2c^2-a′^2}{4}, so a^2=a′^2, and then a=a′, that is, BC=B′C′.
Therefore, AB=A′B′, AC=A′C′, BC=B′C′, and the three sides are equal. According to the SSS judgment, △ABC≌△A′B′C′ is obtained.

stem:
After an earthquake in a certain place, students from Heyan Village Middle School used the following method to check whether the classroom beams were level:

Tie a string to the midpoint of the hypotenuse of an isosceles right-angled triangle, hang a plumb bob on the other end of the string, and attach the hypotenuse of the triangle to the beam. As a result, the string passes through the right-angled vertex of the triangle, and the students are convinced that the beam is horizontal. Were their judgments correct? Why?
stem_lead:
After an earthquake in a certain place, students from Heyan Village Middle School used the following method to check whether the classroom beams were level:

Tie a string to the midpoint of the hypotenuse of an isosceles right-angled triangle, hang a plumb bob on the other end of the string, and attach the hypotenuse of the triangle to the beam. As a result, the string passes through the right-angled vertex of the triangle, and the students are convinced that the beam is horizontal. Were their judgments correct? Why?

mark_scheme.text: right. Because in an isosceles right triangle, the line connecting the midpoint of the hypotenuse and the vertex of the right angle is both the midline of the hypotenuse and the height of the hypotenuse, and must be perpendicular to the hypotenuse; the line (plumb) represents the vertical direction. If the line happens to pass through the vertex of the right angle, the line is a vertical line, so the hypotenuse is perpendicular to the vertical line, that is, the hypotenuse is horizontal and the beams are horizontal.

examiner_comment.text: Attach the hypotenuse of the triangle ruler to the beam, tie a line to the midpoint of the hypotenuse and hang a plumb bob, with the direction of the string being a vertical line. Observe that the string passes through the right-angled vertex, indicating that the line "midpoint of the hypotenuse - right-angled vertex" is vertical. In an isosceles right triangle, the two right-angled sides are equal, and the line connecting the vertex of the right angle to the midpoint of the hypotenuse is the axis of symmetry, so it bisects the hypotenuse and is perpendicular to the hypotenuse (that is, it is the height of the hypotenuse). Since the line is vertical and perpendicular to the hypotenuse, the hypotenuse must be a horizontal line; the hypotenuse is attached to the beam, so the beam is horizontal.

Looking at the lighthouse $C$ from $A$ and $B$, it is measured that $\angle NAC = 42^{\circ}$ and $\angle NBC = 84^{\circ}$. Find the distance from island $B$ to lighthouse $C$.
stem_lead: At 8 o'clock in the morning, a ship departed from the island $A$, sailed due north at a speed of $15\mathrm{~nmile/h}$ (nautical miles per hour, $1\mathrm{~nmile} = 1852\mathrm{~m}$), and arrived at the island $B$ at 10 o'clock. Looking at the lighthouse $C$ from $A$ and $B$, it is measured that $\angle NAC = 42^{\circ}$ and $\angle NBC = 84^{\circ}$. Find the distance from island $B$ to lighthouse $C$.

examiner_comment.text: The ship sails due north from A to B for 2 hours at a speed of 15 knots, so AB=30 knots. Let lighthouse C be on the same side as AB. Taking A as the origin and true north as the positive y-axis, then B(0,30). From ∠NAC=42°, we know that the angle between AC and true north is 42°, so the direction vector of the ray emitted by C at A is (\sin42°,\cos42°); from ∠NBC=84°, we know that the angle between BC and true north is 84°, so the direction vector from B to C is (\sin84°,\cos84°). Assuming BC=s, the C coordinate can also be expressed as (0,30)+s(\sin84°,\cos84°). The two expressions are equal: t\sin42°=s\sin84°, t\cos42°=30+s\cos84°. Eliminate t: s(\sin84°\cot42°-\cos84°)=30. Also \sin84°=\sin(2\cdot42°)=2\sin42°\cos42°, \cos84°=\cos(2\cdot42°)=2\cos^2 42°-1, which can be transformed into =1 in brackets, so s=30.

examiner_comment.text:
An isosceles triangle has two equal angles, and the sum of the interior angles of the triangle is 180°.
(1) If 110° is the base angle, it is impossible that the sum of the two base angles is 220°; therefore 110° is the vertex angle, and the other two angles are equal: (180°−110°)÷2=35°, so they are 35°, 35°.
(2) 80° may be the top or bottom angle:
- If 80° is the vertex angle, then the other two angles are equal: (180°−80°)÷2=50°, which is 50°, 50°;
- If 80° is the base angle, then the other base angle is also 80°, and the vertex angle = 180°−80°−80°=20°, which is 80°, 20°.

stem_lead:
Solve equations and inequalities:

(2) $(3x + 4)(3x - 4) < 9(x - 2)(x + 3)$ .

examiner_comment.text:
(1) Expand and simplify: the left side (x−3)(x−2)+18=x^2−5x+6+18=x^2−5x+24; the right side (x+9)(x+1)=x^2+10x+9. Make both sides equal: x^2−5x+24=x^2+10x+9. Eliminate x^2 to get −5x+24=10x+9, and shift the term to get 15=15x, so x=1.
(2) Expansion: left (3x+4)(3x−4)=9x^2−16; right 9(x−2)(x+3)=9(x^2+x−6)=9x^2+9x−54. Compare: 9x^2−16<9x^2+9x−54, eliminate 9x^2 to get −16<9x−54, add 54 to both sides to get 38<9x, so x>38/9.

Determine the value of $m$ in each of the following equations:

(1) $(x + 4)(x + 9) = x^{2} + mx + 36$
(2) $(x - 2)(x - 18) = x^2 + mx + 36$
(3) $(x + 3)(x + p) = x^{2} + mx + 36$
(4) $(x - 6)(x - p) = x^{2} + mx + 36$
(5) $(x + p)(x + q) = x^{2} + mx + 36$ , $p$ , $q$ are positive integers.
stem_lead:
Determine the value of $m$ in each of the following equations:

(1) $(x + 4)(x + 9) = x^{2} + mx + 36$
(2) $(x - 2)(x - 18) = x^2 + mx + 36$
(3) $(x + 3)(x + p) = x^{2} + mx + 36$
(4) $(x - 6)(x - p) = x^{2} + mx + 36$
(5) $(x + p)(x + q) = x^{2} + mx + 36$ , $p$ , $q$ are positive integers.

examiner_comment.text:
Expand and compare coefficients using the multiplication formula:
(1)(x+4)(x+9)=x^2+(4+9)x+36=x^2+13x+36, so m=13.
(2)(x-2)(x-18)=x^2-(2+18)x+36=x^2-20x+36, so m=-20.
(3)(x+3)(x+p)=x^2+(3+p)x+3p. Comparing with x^2+mx+36, we get 3p=36→p=12, m=3+p=15.
(4)(x-6)(x-p)=x^2-(6+p)x+6p. Compare 6p=36→p=6, m=-(6+p)=-12.
(5)(x+p)(x+q)=x^2+(p+q)x+pq. Compare pq=36, m=p+q. p and q are positive integers, and the pairs of positive factors of 36 are (1,36), (2,18), (3,12), (4,9), (6,6), so m is 37,20,15,13,12 respectively.

stem:
What is wrong with the following calculations? How should it be corrected?

(1) $(a + b)^2 = a^2 + b^2$;

(2) $(a - b)^2 = a^2 - ab + b^2$ .

When calculating using the multiplication formula, sometimes you need to add parentheses in the formula. In Chapter 2, we learned the past bracket rule, which is

$$
a + (b + c) = a + b + c;
$$

$$
a - (b + c) = a - b - c.
$$

In turn, we get the parentheses rule:

$$
a + b + c = a + (b + c);
$$

$$
a - b - c = a - (b + c).
$$

That is to say, when adding parentheses, if the parentheses are preceded by a positive sign, the signs of the items enclosed in the parentheses will not change; if the parentheses are preceded by a negative sign, the signs of the items enclosed by the parentheses will change.

Example 5 Calculate using the multiplication formula:

(1) $(x + 2y - 3)(x - 2y + 3)$ ; (2) $(a + b + c)^2$ .

Solution: (1) $(x + 2y - 3)(x - 2y + 3)$

$$
\begin{array}{l} = [ x + (2 y - 3) ] [ x - (2 y - 3) ] \\ = x ^ {2} - (2 y - 3) ^ {2} \\ = x ^ {2} - (4 y ^ {2} - 1 2 y + 9) \\ = x ^ {2} - 4 y ^ {2} + 1 2 y - 9; \\ \end{array}
$$

(2) $(a + b + c)^2$

$$
\begin{array}{l} = [ (a + b) + c ] ^ {2} \\ = (a + b) ^ {2} + 2 (a + b) c + c ^ {2} \\ = a ^ {2} + 2 a b + b ^ {2} + 2 a c + 2 b c + c ^ {2} \\ = a ^ {2} + b ^ {2} + c ^ {2} + 2 a b + 2 a c + 2 b c. \\ \end{array}
$$

Multiplication of some integers requires appropriate transformation before using the formula.

(1) $(x + 2y - 3)(x - 2y + 3)$ ; (2) $(a + b + c)^2$ .

Solution: (1) $(x + 2y - 3)(x - 2y + 3)$

$$
\begin{array}{l} = [ x + (2 y - 3) ] [ x - (2 y - 3) ] \\ = x ^ {2} - (2 y - 3) ^ {2} \\ = x ^ {2} - (4 y ^ {2} - 1 2 y + 9) \\ = x ^ {2} - 4 y ^ {2} + 1 2 y - 9; \\ \end{array}

$$

mark_scheme.text:
(1) The mistake is that the product term 2ab is omitted from the square formula, which should be changed to: (a+b)^2=a^2+2ab+b^2.

examiner_comment.text: Use the square formula: (a+b)^2=a^2+2ab+b^2, (a-b)^2=a^2-2ab+b^2. In question (1), 2ab is omitted; in question (2), the middle term is written as -ab, and the coefficient is 2 less, so it should be -2ab.

examiner_comment.text:
By\((x+y)(x-y)=x^2-y^2\).
Expand the left side of the first equation: \((x+2)^2-(y-3)^2=(x^2+4x+4)-(y^2-6y+9)=x^2-y^2+4x+6y-5\).
It is equal to the right side \(x^2-y^2\), eliminate \(x^2-y^2\), and get \(4x+6y-5=0\), that is, \(4x+6y=5\).
The second formula is \(x-3y=2\). Simultaneously solve the system of linear equations: From \(x=2+3y\), substitute \(4x+6y=5\): \(4(2+3y)+6y=5\Rightarrow 8+18y=5\Rightarrow y=-\frac{1}{6}\).
Then we get\(x=2+3\left(-\frac{1}{6}\right)=\frac{3}{2}\).

stem_lead:

(1) $x^{2} + y^{2}$

(2) $x^{2} - y^{2}$

(3) $-x^{2} + y^{2}$

(4) $-x^{2} - y^{2}$

mark_scheme.text:
(1) No, the squared difference formula applies to the form a^2-b^2, x^2+y^2 is not a difference.
(2) Energy, x^2-y^2=(x+y)(x-y).
(3) Energy, -x^2+y^2=y^2-x^2=(y+x)(y-x).
(4) No, -x^2-y^2=-(x^2+y^2) is still in the form of sum, not square difference.

examiner_comment.text:
The formula for square difference is a^2-b^2=(a+b)(a-b). The key is "the difference of two squares".
(1)x^2+y^2 is the sum of two squares, which is inconsistent.
(2) is directly the difference of two squares, which can be decomposed into (x+y)(x-y).
(3)-x^2+y^2 can be written in commutative order as y^2-x^2, which is the difference of two squares and is decomposed into (y+x)(y-x).
(4)-x^2-y^2=-(x^2+y^2), the sum of squares is still in the brackets, which does not conform to the square difference structure, so it cannot be decomposed by the square difference formula.

examiner_comment.text:
The completely flat method needs to be able to be written as (x±y)^2=x^2±2xy+y^2. Inspection item by item:

(3) Suppose 4b^2+4b-1=(2b+c)^2=4b^2+4cb+c^2. The comparison shows that c=1, but the constant term should be 1, which is inconsistent with -1.
(4) Suppose a^2+ab+b^2=(a+kb)^2=a^2+2kab+k^2b^2. The comparison shows that k=1/2, but k^2=1/4 does not match the b^2 coefficient of 1, so it is not a perfect square method.

Observe the following formula:

$$
\begin{array}{l} 2 \times 4 + 1 = 9 = 3 ^ {2}; \\ 6 \times 8 + 1 = 4 9 = 7 ^ {2}; \\ 1 4 \times 1 6 + 1 = 2 2 5 = 1 5 ^ {2}; \\ \dots \\ \end{array}
$$

What conclusion did you draw? Can you prove this conclusion?

mark_scheme.text: Conclusion: Any two even numbers that differ by 2 multiplied by 1 are equal to the square of the odd number between them. That is, for any positive integer n, there is \((2n)(2n+2)+1=(2n+1)^2\).

stem:
The price of raw materials for a certain product has increased, so the manufacturer decides to increase the price of the product. There are three options:

(1) The first price increase is $p\%$, and the second price increase is $q\%$
(2) The first price increase is $q\%$, and the second price increase is $p\%$
(3) The first and second price increases are both $\frac{p + q}{2}\%$.

Among them, $p, q$ are unequal positive numbers. Which of the three options increases the price the most?

(Hint: Since $p \neq q$ , $(p - q)^2 = p^2 - 2pq + q^2 > 0$ , so $p^2 + q^2 > 2pq$ )
stem_lead:
The price of raw materials for a certain product has increased, so the manufacturer decides to increase the price of the product. There are three options:

(1) The first price increase is $p\%$, and the second price increase is $q\%$
(2) The first price increase is $q\%$, and the second price increase is $p\%$
(3) The first and second price increases are both $\frac{p + q}{2}\%$.

Among them, $p, q$ are unequal positive numbers. Which of the three options increases the price the most?

(Hint: Since $p \neq q$ , $(p - q)^2 = p^2 - 2pq + q^2 > 0$ , so $p^2 + q^2 > 2pq$ )

mark_scheme.text: Option (3) has the largest price increase (Option (1) is the same as Option (2) and smaller than Option (3)).

examiner_comment.text:
Let the original price be 1.
Option (1): Final price = (1+p/100)(1+q/100)=1+(p+q)/100+pq/10000.
Solution (2): (1+q/100)(1+p/100) is the same as solution (1).
Option (3): Final price = (1+(p+q)/200)^2=1+(p+q)/100+(p+q)^2/40000.
Compare the incremental terms of schemes (1) and (3): pq/10000 and (p+q)^2/40000.
Multiply by 40000 to get: 4pq and (p+q)^2=p^2+2pq+q^2.
Since p≠q and is a positive number, (p-q)^2>0 ⇒ p^2+q^2>2pq ⇒ p^2+2pq+q^2>4pq.
Therefore (p+q)^2/40000>pq/10000, the final price of option (3) is greater.

$$

stem_lead:
Which of the following formulas are fractions? What are the integers? What is the difference between the two types of expressions?

$$
\frac {1}{x}, \frac {x}{3}, \frac {4}{3 b ^ {3} + 5}, \frac {2 a - 5}{3}, \frac {x}{x ^ {2} - y ^ {2}}, \frac {m - n}{m + n}, \frac {x ^ {2} + 2 x + 1}{x ^ {2} - 2 x + 1}, \frac {c}{3 (a - b)}.
$$

mark_scheme.text:
Fraction: \(\frac{1}{x},\ \frac{4}{3b^{3}+5},\ \frac{x}{x^{2}-y^{2}},\ \frac{m-n}{m+n},\ \frac{x^{2}+2x+1}{x^{2}-2x+1},\ \frac{c}{3(a-b)}\).
Integer formula: \(\frac{x}{3},\ \frac{2a-5}{3}\) (all can be written as \(\frac13x\), \(\frac13(2a-5)\), the denominator is a constant).
The difference: the integer does not contain letters in the denominator (can be regarded as the denominator is 1 or other constants), and is a polynomial; the fraction is the division of two integers and the denominator contains letters (the denominator is not a constant), and the denominator cannot be 0.

mark_scheme.text: The ship sailed against the current t h and traveled \(\dfrac{pnt}{qm}\) km.

examiner_comment.text: Downstream speed \(v_\text{Downward}=\dfrac{n}{m}\) (km/h). Sailing against the current is a distance of \(t\) hours \(s=v_\text{counter}\cdot t=\dfrac{pn}{qm}\cdot t=\dfrac{pnt}{qm}\) (km).

stem: Transplanting rice on a rice field of $a \mathrm{hm}^2$, if 10 people transplant, it will take $m$ days to complete; if a rice transplanter works, it will be completed 3 days earlier than if 10 people transplant. How many times the working efficiency of a rice transplanter is that of one person?
stem_lead: Transplanting rice on a rice field of $a \mathrm{hm}^2$, if 10 people transplant, it will take $m$ days to complete; if a rice transplanter works, it will be completed 3 days earlier than if 10 people transplant. How many times the working efficiency of a rice transplanter is that of one person?

examiner_comment.text:
Let the work efficiency of one person be x (the area completed by each person per day).
10 people can complete it in m days: a=10x·m, so x=a/(10m).
The rice transplanter completes the work 3 days ahead of the 10 people, so it takes m-3 days: the efficiency of the rice transplanter is a/(m-3).
The ratio of the efficiency of the rice transplanter to the efficiency of one person is: \frac{a/(m-3)}{a/(10m)}=\frac{10m}{m-3}.

stem: A wheat field has an area of ​​$m \, \mathrm{hm}^2$. A needs $n \, \mathrm{h}$ to harvest the wheat field. B can harvest the wheat field with $0.5 \, \mathrm{h}$ less than A. How many hours will it take for the two to harvest the wheat field together?
stem_lead: A wheat field has an area of ​​$m \, \mathrm{hm}^2$. A needs $n \, \mathrm{h}$ to harvest the wheat field. B can harvest the wheat field with $0.5 \, \mathrm{h}$ less than A. How many hours will it take for the two to harvest the wheat field together?

mark_scheme.text: It takes two people to harvest together\(\dfrac{n(n-0.5)}{2n-0.5}\,\text{h}=\dfrac{n(2n-1)}{4n-1}\,\text{h}\).

examiner_comment.text: A's efficiency is \(\frac{m}{n}\,\text{hm}^2/\text{h}\), B takes \(n-0.5\) hours, and the efficiency is \(\frac{m}{n-0.5}\). The cooperation efficiency of two people\(\frac{m}{n}+\frac{m}{n-0.5}=m\left(\frac{1}{n}+\frac{1}{n-0.5}\right)\). Suppose the cooperation time is \(t\), then \(m=t\cdot m\left(\frac{1}{n}+\frac{1}{n-0.5}\right)\), so \(t=\frac{1}{\frac{1}{n}+\frac{1}{n-0.5}}=\frac{n(n-0.5)}{2n-0.5}=\frac{n(2n-1)}{4n-1}\) hours.

stem:
The volume of an uncovered rectangular box is $V$ .

(1) If the bottom of the box is a square with side length $a$, what is the surface area of the box?  
(2) If the bottom of the box is a rectangle with length $b$ and width $c$, what is the surface area of the box?
(3) In the above two cases, if the bottom areas of the boxes are equal, what is the difference in the surface areas of the two boxes?

(Excluding the thickness of the manufacturing material.)
stem_lead:
The volume of an uncovered rectangular box is $V$ .

(1) If the bottom of the box is a square with side length $a$, what is the surface area of the box?  
(2) If the bottom of the box is a rectangle with length $b$ and width $c$, what is the surface area of the box?
(3) In the above two cases, if the bottom areas of the boxes are equal, what is the difference in the surface areas of the two boxes?

(Excluding the thickness of the manufacturing material.)

mark_scheme.text:
(1) The base is a square with side length a: height h=V/a^2, surface area S=a^2+4ah=a^2+4V/a.
(2) A rectangle with a base of b×c: height h=V/(bc), surface area S=bc+2bh+2ch=bc+2V/c+2V/b.
(3) If the bottom areas are equal (a^2=bc), the difference in surface area of ​​the two boxes is ΔS=(a^2+4V/a)−(bc+2V/b+2V/c)=4V/a−2V/b−2V/c (the absolute value of the difference is taken).

examiner_comment.text:
The surface area of ​​a cuboid box without a lid = the area of ​​the base + the area of ​​the four sides. First, find the height from the volume V = bottom area × height:
(1) The bottom area a^2→h=V/a^2; there are 4 side areas in total, each with an area a·h, so S=a^2+4ah=a^2+4V/a.
(2) The bottom area bc→h=V/(bc); the area of ​​the two side pieces is b·h, and the area of ​​the two pieces is c·h, so S=bc+2bh+2ch=bc+2V/c+2V/b.
(3) If a^2=bc, the bottom area terms cancel, and only the side area terms are compared, the difference ΔS=4V/a−2V/b−2V/c is obtained. When asking about "phase difference", take |ΔS|.

After the water surface reaches half the height of the container, a large water pipe with a diameter twice as large as the small water pipe is used to fill the container with water. The total process of filling the container with water takes a total time of $t \mathrm{~min}$. Find the water filling speed of each of the two water pipes. (Hint: Consider how many times the water filling speed of the large water pipe is the water filling speed of the small water pipe.)
stem_lead: The volume of a cylindrical container is $V \mathrm{~m}^{3}$. A small water pipe is used to fill the container with water. After the water surface reaches half the height of the container, a large water pipe with a diameter twice as large as the small water pipe is used to fill the container with water. The total process of filling the container with water takes a total time of $t \mathrm{~min}$. Find the water filling speed of each of the two water pipes. (Hint: Consider how many times the water filling speed of the large water pipe is the water filling speed of the small water pipe.)

mark_scheme.text: The water injection speed of the small water pipe is \(\dfrac{5V}{8t}\,\text{m}^3/\text{min}\), and the water injection speed of the large water pipe is \(\dfrac{5V}{2t}\,\text{m}^3/\text{min}\).

examiner_comment.text: Let the water injection speed of the small water pipe be \(x\,\text{m}^3/\text{min}\). The diameter of the large water pipe is twice that of the small water pipe, and the cross-sectional area is proportional to the square of the diameter, so the speed of the large water pipe is \(4x\). The corresponding volume from the water surface to half the height of the cylindrical container is \(\frac V2\). The first half uses small water pipe time \(t_1=\frac{V/2}{x}=\frac{V}{2x}\); the second half uses large water pipe time \(t_2=\frac{V/2}{4x}=\frac{V}{8x}\). The total time \(t=t_1+t_2=\frac{V}{2x}+\frac{V}{8x}=\frac{5V}{8x}\), the solution is \(x=\frac{5V}{8t}\). Therefore the large water pipe velocity \(4x=\frac{5V}{2t}\).

mark_scheme.text: The original average yield per hectare was \(\frac{am}{20}\) t, and now the average yield per hectare is \(\frac{a(m+20)}{20}\) t.

examiner_comment.text: Assuming that the original average yield per hectare is \(x\) t, then the land area is \(\frac{m}{x}\) hectares. After improvement, the average increase per hectare is \(a\) t, and now the average per hectare is \(x+a\) t, so the current total output is \((x+a)\cdot\frac{m}{x}=m+20\). Simplify to get\(m\left(1+\frac{a}{x}\right)=m+20\), then\(\frac{am}{x}=20\), and solve to get\(x=\frac{am}{20}\). Therefore, the average yield per hectare is now \(x+a=\frac{am}{20}+a=\frac{a(m+20)}{20}\).

(1) The speed of the second group is 5 m/min, and the speed of the first group is 6 m/min.
(2) Assume the second set of speeds is v2, then the first set of speeds v1 = a v2. From h/v2 - h/(a v2)=t, v2= h(a-1)/(a t), v1= h(a-1)/t (unit: m/min, t is measured in min).

examiner_comment.text:
(1) Assume the speed of the second group is x (m/min), then the speed of the first group is 1.2x. The peaking times are T2=450/x and T1=450/(1.2x) respectively. It is known that T2−T1=15: 450/x−450/(1.2x)=15 ⇒ 450/x−375/x=15 ⇒ 75/x=15 ⇒ x=5, so the second group is 5 m/min and the first group is 1.2×5=6 m/min.
(2) Assume the second set of speed v2, the first set of v1 = a v2. Time difference: h/v2−h/v1=t ⇒ h/v2−h/(a v2)=t ⇒ h(1−1/a)/v2=t ⇒ v2=h(a−1)/(a t), v1=a v2=h(a−1)/t.

mark_scheme.text:
Example word problem: Two people, A and B, cooperate to complete a task. It is known that it takes B 6 hours longer to complete the task than A alone, and it takes 4 hours for the two of them to complete the task together. Find how many hours it will take A and B to complete the project alone.
Answer: It takes A 6 hours to complete it alone, and it takes 12 hours for B to complete it alone.

examiner_comment.text:
Suppose A alone takes x hours to complete, then B alone takes (x+6) hours to complete. It takes two people 4 hours to complete the work, and the work efficiency is: 1/x + 1/(x+6) = 1/4.
The common score is: (2x+6)/[x(x+6)] = 1/4, and the cross multiplication is: 4(2x+6)=x(x+6).
Simplify: 8x+24=x^2+6x, move terms: x^2-2x-24=0, factorize: (x-6)(x+4)=0.
Take the positive value x=6 (x=-4 is discarded). So A has 6 hours, and B x+6=12 hours.

stem: A car drives to a destination $180 \mathrm{~km}$ away from the departure point. It drives at a constant speed at the original planned speed in the first hour after departure. After one hour, it drives at a constant speed 1.5 times the original speed and reaches the destination $40 \mathrm{~min}$ earlier than the original plan. Find the driving speed during the previous hour.
stem_lead: A car drives to a destination $180 \mathrm{~km}$ away from the departure point. It drives at a constant speed at the original planned speed in the first hour after departure. After one hour, it drives at a constant speed 1.5 times the original speed and reaches the destination $40 \mathrm{~min}$ earlier than the original plan. Find the driving speed during the previous hour.

examiner_comment.text: Let the original planned speed be v(km/h). The original planned time is T=180/v(h). Actual trip: travel v km in the first hour, and travel at 1.5v for the remaining (180−v) km, taking (180−v)/(1.5v) h. Therefore, the actual time T'=1+(180−v)/(1.5v). And because it arrived 40 minutes=2/3 hours earlier, T'=T−2/3. Series equation: 1+(180−v)/(1.5v)=180/v−2/3. Simplify: (180−v)/(1.5v)=120/v−2/3, so the left side is 1+120/v−2/3=1/3+120/v. So 1/3+120/v=180/v−2/3, we get 1=60/v, and the solution is v=60(km/h).

examiner_comment.text:
(1) Original formula =\(\frac{(x-1)(x+1)}{(x-1)^2}\div\frac{x+1}{x-1}\cdot\frac{1-x}{1+x}\)=\ (\frac{x+1}{x-1}\cdot\frac{x-1}{x+1}\cdot\frac{1-x}{1+x}\)=\(\frac{1-x}{1+x}= -\frac{x-1}{x+1}\). Substituting \(x=\frac12\), we get\(-\frac{-1/2}{3/2}=\frac13\).
(2)\(\frac{x^2-4x+4}{x^2-4}\div\frac{x-2}{x^2+2x}+3=\frac{(x-2)^2}{(x-2)(x+ 2)}\div\frac{x-2}{x(x+2)}+3=\frac{x-2}{x+2}\cdot\frac{x(x+2)}{x-2}+3=x+3\). Substituting \(x=-3.2\), we get \(-3.2+3=-0.2\).

stem:
(1) Can the value of the formula $\frac{a}{bc} + \frac{b}{ca} + \frac{c}{ab}$ be 0? Why?
(2) Can the value of the formula $\frac{a - b}{(b - c)(c - a)} + \frac{b - c}{(a - b)(c - a)} + \frac{c - a}{(a - b)(b - c)}$ be 0? Why?
stem_lead:
(1) Can the value of the formula $\frac{a}{bc} + \frac{b}{ca} + \frac{c}{ab}$ be 0? Why?
(2) Can the value of the formula $\frac{a - b}{(b - c)(c - a)} + \frac{b - c}{(a - b)(c - a)} + \frac{c - a}{(a - b)(b - c)}$ be 0? Why?

mark_scheme.text:
(1) cannot be 0. Because\( rac{a}{bc}+ rac{b}{ca}+ rac{c}{ab}= rac{a^2+b^2+c^2}{abc}\). Under the premise of \(a,b,c
eq0\), the denominator \(abc
eq0\); if the value is 0, then \(a^2+b^2+c^2=0\) is required. In the range of real numbers, only \(a=b=c=0\) can be derived, which is inconsistent with the fact that the denominator is not 0.
(2) cannot be 0. Divide each term into \((a-b)(b-c)(c-a)\): original formula =\( rac{(a-b)^2+(b-c)^2+(c-a)^2}{(a-b)(b-c)(c-a)}\). The denominator requires \(a
eq b
eq c
eq a\) to make it non-0; if the original formula is 0, the numerator needs to be 0, that is, \((a-b)^2+(b-c)^2+(c-a)^2=0\). In the range of real numbers, only \(a=b=c\) can be derived, but this will make the denominator 0, which is a contradiction.

examiner_comment.text:
(1) Write each item with the same denominator: \(\frac{a}{bc}=\frac{a^2}{abc}\), \(\frac{b}{ca}=\frac{b^2}{abc}\), \(\frac{c}{ab}=\frac{c^2}{abc}\), so the sum is \(\frac{a^2+b^2+c^2}{abc}\). When the real number is \(a,b,c\neq0\), \(a^2+b^2+c^2>0\), it cannot be 0.
(2) Let the common denominator\(D=(a-b)(b-c)(c-a)\). Then \(\frac{a-b}{(b-c)(c-a)}=\frac{(a-b)^2}{D}\), \(\frac{b-c}{(a-b)(c-a )}=\frac{(b-c)^2}{D}\), \(\frac{c-a}{(a-b)(b-c)}=\frac{(c-a)^2}{D}\). Adding them together gives \(\frac{(a-b)^2+(b-c)^2+(c-a)^2}{D}\). The numerator is 0 only when \(a=b=c\), but at this time \(D=0\) does not hold, so the original formula cannot be 0.

After experiments, it is found that $h$ is directly proportional to $t^2$, and when $h = 20$, $t = 2$. Use $h$ to represent $t$, and find out when $h = 10$ and $h = 25$ respectively. , the time it takes for the ball to hit the ground.
stem_lead: The ball falls freely from a height of $h$ (unit: m) from the ground, and the time it takes to fall to the ground is $t$ (unit: s). After experiments, it is found that $h$ is directly proportional to $t^2$, and when $h = 20$, $t = 2$. Use $h$ to represent $t$, and find out when $h = 10$ and $h = 25$ respectively. , the time it takes for the ball to hit the ground.

mark_scheme.text: Since h is proportional to t^2, let h=kt^2. From h=20, t=2, we get 20=4k, k=5, so t=\sqrt{h/5}. When h=10, t=\sqrt{10/5}=\sqrt2(s); when h=25, t=\sqrt{25/5}=\sqrt5(s).

examiner_comment.text: From "h is proportional to t^2", we get h=kt^2. Substituting the known point (20,2): 20=k·(2^2)=4k, the solution is k=5. So h=5t^2, solve t=\sqrt{h/5}(t>0). Then substitute h=10 and 25 respectively to calculate \sqrt2 and \sqrt5.

stem_lead:
(1) It is known that $\sqrt{18 - n}$ is an integer, find all possible values of the natural number $n$;
(2) It is known that $\sqrt{24n}$ is an integer, find the minimum value of the positive integer $n$

mark_scheme.text: (1) n=2, 9, 14, 17, 18; (2) The minimum value of n is 6

examiner_comment.text:
(1) Assume 18-n=k^2 (k is a non-negative integer), then k^2≤18, k^2 can be 0, 1, 4, 9, 16, corresponding to n=18, 17, 14, 9, 2. Therefore n∈{2, 9, 14, 17, 18}.
(2) 24n is a perfect square number. Decompose 24=2^3·3. To make the exponents all even numbers, you need to add another 2 and a 3, that is, n contains at least 2·3=6. At this time, 24·6=144=12^2, which satisfies the condition. Therefore, n is at least 6.

mark_scheme.text: r=\sqrt{\dfrac{V}{10\pi}}; when V=5\pi, r=\sqrt{\dfrac{1}{2}}=\dfrac{\sqrt2}{2}; when V=10\pi, r=1; when V=20\pi, r=\sqrt2.

examiner_comment.text: The formula for the volume of a cylinder is V=\pi r^2 h. It is known that h=10, then V=\pi r^2\cdot10=10\pi r^2, so r^2=\dfrac{V}{10\pi}, r=\sqrt{\dfrac{V}{10\pi}} (the radius is taken as positive). Substitute: V=5\pi to get r=\sqrt{\dfrac{5\pi}{10\pi}}=\sqrt{\dfrac12}=\dfrac{\sqrt2}{2}; V=10\p i gets r=\sqrt{\dfrac{10\pi}{10\pi}}=1; V=20\pi gets r=\sqrt{\dfrac{20\pi}{10\pi}}=\sqrt2.

stem:
Are the following calculations correct? Why?

(1) $\sqrt{8} -\sqrt{3} = \sqrt{8 - 3}$
(2) $\sqrt{4} +\sqrt{9} = \sqrt{4 + 9}$
(3) $3\sqrt{2} - \sqrt{2} = 2\sqrt{2}$ .
stem_lead:
Are the following calculations correct? Why?

(1) $\sqrt{8} -\sqrt{3} = \sqrt{8 - 3}$
(2) $\sqrt{4} +\sqrt{9} = \sqrt{4 + 9}$
(3) $3\sqrt{2} - \sqrt{2} = 2\sqrt{2}$ .

mark_scheme.text:
(1) is incorrect. Because in general, √a±√b≠√(a±b), such as √8−√3≈2.828−1.732≈1.096, and √(8−3)=√5≈2.236, are not equal.
(2) is incorrect. Because in general, √a+√b≠√(a+b), such as √4+√9=2+3=5, and √(4+9)=√13≈3.606, are not equal.
(3) Correct. Because similar quadratic radicals can be combined: 3√2−√2=(3−1)√2=2√2.

examiner_comment.text: Determine whether the radical operation can "add and subtract the radicals": √a·√b=√(ab) (a, b≥0) can only be used for multiplication and division. Addition and subtraction cannot be combined into the same radical; but similar quadratic radicals (the same within the radical) can combine coefficients like similar terms. Therefore (1)(2) is wrong and (3) is correct.

It is known that the resistance of the wire is $5\Omega$, and the wire generates 30J of heat in 1s. Find the value of the current $I$ (retain the result to two decimal places).

examiner_comment.text: From Joule's law Q=I^2Rt, substitute R=5Ω, t=1s, Q=30J: 30=I^2×5×1, and get I^2=30/5=6, so I=√6≈2.449, which is 2.45A with two decimal places.

examiner_comment.text: Decompose prime factors: 189=3^3×7. To make √(189n) an integer, 189n must be a perfect square number, that is, the exponent of each prime factor in prime factorization is an even number. The current exponent of 3 is 3 (odd number), add 1 3 to make it 4; the exponent of 7 is 1 (odd number), add 1 7 to make it 2. Therefore, the minimum n=3×7=21, at this time 189n=3^4×7^2=(3^2×7)^2 is a perfect square number.

stem:
Determine whether the following expressions are true:

$$
\sqrt {2 \frac {2}{3}} = 2 \sqrt {\frac {2}{3}}; \quad \sqrt {3 \frac {3}{8}} = 3 \sqrt {\frac {3}{8}}; \quad \sqrt {4 \frac {4}{1 5}} = 4 \sqrt {\frac {4}{1 5}}.
$$

By analogy with the above formula, write several formulas of the same type. Can you see the pattern? Represent this rule with a letter and give a proof.
stem_lead:
Determine whether the following expressions are true:

$$
\sqrt {2 \frac {2}{3}} = 2 \sqrt {\frac {2}{3}}; \quad \sqrt {3 \frac {3}{8}} = 3 \sqrt {\frac {3}{8}}; \quad \sqrt {4 \frac {4}{1 5}} = 4 \sqrt {\frac {4}{1 5}}.
$$

By analogy with the above formula, write several formulas of the same type. Can you see the pattern? Represent this rule with a letter and give a proof.

mark_scheme.text: All three equations hold. It can be written by analogy: \(\sqrt{5\frac{5}{24}}=5\sqrt{\frac{5}{24}}\), \(\sqrt{6\frac{6}{3 5}}=6\sqrt{\frac{6}{35}}\),\(\sqrt{7\frac{7}{48}}=7\sqrt{\frac{7}{48}}\) Wait. Rule: For any integer \(n\ge2\), there is \(\sqrt{n\frac{n}{n^2-1}}=n\sqrt{\frac{n}{n^2-1}}\).

examiner_comment.text:
First judge the original form:
1) \(2\frac{2}{3}=\frac{8}{3}\), the right side \(2\sqrt{\frac23}=\sqrt{4\cdot\frac23}=\sqrt{\frac83}\), both sides are equal.
2) \(3\frac{3}{8}=\frac{27}{8}\), the right side \(3\sqrt{\frac38}=\sqrt{9\cdot\frac38}=\sqrt{\frac{27}{8}}\), both sides are equal.
3) \(4\frac{4}{15}=\frac{64}{15}\), the right side \(4\sqrt{\frac4{15}}=\sqrt{16\cdot\frac4{15}}=\sqrt{\frac{64}{15}}\), both sides are equal.

Observe the denominator: \(3=2^2-1,\ 8=3^2-1,\ 15=4^2-1\). Therefore, the same type of formula is \(\sqrt{n\frac{n}{n^2-1}}=n\sqrt{\frac{n}{n^2-1}}\).
Proof: left
\[
\sqrt{n\frac{n}{n^2-1}}=\sqrt{n+\frac{n}{n^2-1}}=\sqrt{\frac{n(n^2-1)+n}{n^2-1}}=\sqrt{\frac{n^3}{n^2-1}}.
\]
right
\[
 n\sqrt{\frac{n}{n^2-1}}=\sqrt{n^2\cdot\frac{n}{n^2-1}}=\sqrt{\frac{n^3}{n^2-1}}.
\]
Both sides are \(\sqrt{\frac{n^3}{n^2-1}}\), so it is always true (the denominator is not 0 when \(n\ge2\)).

When $x$ is what kind of real number, do the following expressions make sense in the range of real numbers?

(1) $\sqrt{3 + x}$

(2) $\frac{1}{\sqrt{2x - 1}}$

(3) $\sqrt{\frac{1}{2 - 3x}}$ ;

(4) $\sqrt{\frac{1}{(x - 1)^2}}$ .
stem_lead:
When $x$ is what kind of real number, do the following expressions make sense in the range of real numbers?

(1) $\sqrt{3 + x}$

(2) $\frac{1}{\sqrt{2x - 1}}$

(3) $\sqrt{\frac{1}{2 - 3x}}$ ;

(4) $\sqrt{\frac{1}{(x - 1)^2}}$ .

examiner_comment.text:
Conditions that are meaningful within the range of real numbers: ≥0 within the root sign, and the denominator ≠0.
(1) 3+x≥0 ⇒ x≥-3.
(2) The denominator is √(2x-1), which requires 2x-1>0 (both to ensure that the root sign is non-negative and that the denominator is not 0) ⇒ x>1/2.
(3) 1/(2-3x)≥0 and 2-3x≠0 are required. Since the numerator 1>0, it requires 2-3x>0 ⇒ x<2/3.
(4) It requires 1/(x-1)^2≥0 and (x-1)^2≠0. The square is constant ≥ 0 and is 0 if and only if x=1, which will make the denominator 0, so x≠1.

If the reed is pulled toward the midpoint of one side of the pool, its top will just reach the water at the edge of the pool. What is the depth of the water and the length of the reed?

This is a question in the an ancient mathematics text "Nine Chapters of Arithmetic". The original text is: Today there is a pond with a square foot, and a chia grows in the center, and the water is one foot. Lead the chia to the shore, and it will be flush with the bank. Ask about the depth of the water and the length of the chia. (Zhang and chi are units of length, 1 chi $= 10$ chi, $1$ chi $= \frac{1}{3}$ m.)

mark_scheme.text: The water is 12 feet deep and the reeds are 13 feet long.

examiner_comment.text: Assume the water depth is x feet, then the total length of the reeds is x+1 feet (1 foot above the water surface). The sides of the pool are 10 feet long. The reed is in the center and stretched to the midpoint of one side. The horizontal distance is 10/2=5 feet. At this time, the vertical height x from the reeds, the bottom of the pool to the water surface, and the horizontal distance 5 form a right triangle, so (x+1)^2=x^2+5^2. Expand to get x^2+2x+1=x^2+25, simplify 2x=24 and get x=12. The length of the reed is x+1=13 feet.

stem: A wooden pole broke at a distance of $3 \mathrm{~m}$ from the ground, and the top of the wooden pole fell at a distance of $4 \mathrm{~m}$ from the bottom of the wooden pole. How high was the wooden pole before it broke?
stem_lead: A wooden pole broke at a distance of $3 \mathrm{~m}$ from the ground, and the top of the wooden pole fell at a distance of $4 \mathrm{~m}$ from the bottom of the wooden pole. How high was the wooden pole before it broke?

examiner_comment.text: The wooden pole breaks 3m above the ground. The vertical distance from the breaking point to the ground is 3m; the horizontal distance from the top landing point to the bottom of the wooden pole is 4m. The broken upper half forms the hypotenuse of a right triangle with a length of √(3^2+4^2)=5m. The original length of the wooden pole = 3m in the lower half + 5m in the upper half = 8m.

stem: We know that 3, 4, and 5 are a set of Pythagorean numbers, so are $3k, 4k, 5k$ ($k$ is a positive integer) also a set of Pythagorean numbers? In general, if $a, b, c$ is a set of Pythagorean numbers, then $ak, bk, ck$ ($k$ is a positive integer) are also a set of Pythagorean numbers?
stem_lead: We know that 3, 4, and 5 are a set of Pythagorean numbers, so are $3k, 4k, 5k$ ($k$ is a positive integer) also a set of Pythagorean numbers? In general, if $a, b, c$ is a set of Pythagorean numbers, then $ak, bk, ck$ ($k$ is a positive integer) are also a set of Pythagorean numbers?

mark_scheme.text: yes. Because 3^2+4^2=5^2, multiply both sides by k^2 to get (3k)^2+(4k)^2=(5k)^2; generally, if a^2+b^2=c^2, then (ak)^2+(bk)^2=(ck)^2, so ak, bk, ck are also a set of Pythagorean numbers (k is a positive integer).

examiner_comment.text: Pythagorean definition: Positive integers a, b, c satisfy a^2+b^2=c^2. It is known that 3^2+4^2=5^2. For any positive integer k, calculate (3k)^2+(4k)^2=9k^2+16k^2=25k^2=(5k)^2, so 3k, 4k, and 5k still satisfy the Pythagorean relationship. Generally, if a^2+b^2=c^2, then multiply both sides by k^2: k^2(a^2+b^2)=k^2c^2, that is, (ak)^2+(bk)^2=(ck)^2, and ak, bk, ck are still positive integers, so it is still a set of Pythagorean numbers.

stem: If the lengths of three line segments $a, b, c$ satisfy $a^2 = c^2 - b^2$, is the triangle formed by these three line segments a right triangle? Why?
stem_lead: If the lengths of three line segments $a, b, c$ satisfy $a^2 = c^2 - b^2$, is the triangle formed by these three line segments a right triangle? Why?

mark_scheme.text: It is a right triangle (with c as the hypotenuse). Because from a^2=c^2-b^2, we can get a^2+b^2=c^2. If a, b, and c can form a triangle, then according to the converse theorem of the Pythagorean theorem, the triangle is a right-angled triangle, and the right angle faces side c.

examiner_comment.text: From the question, suppose a^2=c^2-b^2, and add b^2 to both sides to get a^2+b^2=c^2. If the line segments a, b, and c can form a triangle (the sum of any two sides is greater than the third side), and c is the longest side, then the conditions of the converse theorem of the Pythagorean theorem are met: the sum of the squares of the two right-angled sides is equal to the square of the third side, so the triangle is a right-angled triangle, with the right angle sandwiched between a and b, and c is the hypotenuse.

mark_scheme.text:
(1) Converse proposition: the internal angles are equal and the two straight lines are parallel; established (under the premise that the two straight lines are intercepted by a third straight line).
(2) Converse proposition: If the absolute values ​​of two real numbers are equal, then the two real numbers are equal; this is not true (such as 1 and -1).
(3) Converse proposition: If the corresponding angles of two triangles are equal, then the two triangles are congruent; this is not true (it can only be inferred that they are similar, not necessarily congruent).
(4) Converse proposition: The distance from a point on the bisector of an angle to both sides of the angle is equal; established.

examiner_comment.text: The way to write a converse proposition is to exchange the "condition" and "conclusion". (1) It belongs to the parallel line determination theorem: the internal angles are equal ⇒ the two straight lines are parallel (need to have a cross-section situation), so it is established. (2) |a|=|b| can only deduce a=b or a=-b, so it is not true. (3) Equality of corresponding angles only ensures that the two triangles are similar, but the side lengths are not necessarily equal, so it is not true. (4) Properties of angle bisectors: The distances from points on the bisector to both sides are equal, so the converse proposition is true.

mark_scheme.text:
(1) Converse proposition: If two straight lines are parallel, then the interior angles on the same side are complementary. established.
(2) Converse proposition: If two angles are equal, then they are both right angles. Not established.
(3) Converse proposition: If the corresponding sides of two triangles are equal, then the two triangles are congruent. established.
(4) Converse proposition: If the squares of two real numbers are equal, then the two real numbers are equal. Not established.

examiner_comment.text:
To write a converse proposition is to reverse the "conditions" and "conclusion" of the original proposition.
(1) Properties of parallel lines: Two straight lines are parallel and interior angles on the same side are complementary, so the converse statement is true.
(2) Two equal angles are not necessarily right angles (they can be any equal angles), so the converse statement is false.
(3) If the corresponding three sides are equal, it can be concluded that the triangles are congruent (SSS judgment), so the converse proposition is true.
(4) x^2=y^2 can only deduce x=y or x=-y, such as 1^2=(-1)^2, so the converse statement is false.

mark_scheme.text: North or south (direction perpendicular to east)

examiner_comment.text: Assume that the starting point is A and 80 m eastward to B, then AB=80. Then walk to C, BC=60, and finally return to A from C, CA=100. Use the cosine theorem from triangle ABC: CA^2=AB^2+BC^2−2·AB·BC·cos∠ABC, that is, 100^2=80^2+60^2−2·80·60·cos∠ABC. The calculation is 10000=10000−9600cos∠ABC, so cos∠ABC=0, ∠ABC=90°. Therefore, the second section of road BC is perpendicular to the eastward AB, and the direction can only be north or south.

examiner_comment.text: Assume that the height of the broken point from the ground is x feet, then the length of the upper section of bamboo is (10−x) feet (because 1 foot = 10 feet). After breaking, the top of the upper section of bamboo falls to the ground, and the landing point is 3 feet away from the bottom of the bamboo, forming a right-angled triangle: the right-angled sides are x and 3, and the hypotenuse is (10-x). According to the Pythagorean theorem: (10−x)^2=x^2+3^2. Expanding it, we get 100−20x+x^2=x^2+9, and simplifying it, we get 100−20x=9, so 20x=91, x=91/20 feet.

mark_scheme.text: right. Because when m>1 is an integer, let a=2m, b=m^2-1, c=m^2+1, then a^2+b^2=c^2, so (a, b, c) is the Pythagorean number. Example: m=2 gets (4,3,5); m=3 gets (6,8,10); m=4 gets (8,15,17); m=5 gets (10,24,26).

examiner_comment.text: To verify whether it is a Pythagorean number, you only need to check whether a^2+b^2 is equal to c^2: a^2+b^2=(2m)^2+(m^2-1)^2=4m^2+(m^4-2m^2+1)=m^4+2m^2+1=(m^2+1)^2=c^2, so the conclusion is established. Then substitute different integers m to generate the Pythagorean array.

examiner_comment.text: Whether a wooden stick can be put into a rectangular wooden box depends on whether the longest straight line segment (space diagonal) in the wooden box is not less than the length of the wooden stick. Then from the prompt "height is perpendicular to any straight line on the base", the space diagonal d=√(d_base^2+30^2)=√(4100+900)=√5000≈70.71 (cm). Because 70<70.71, the 70 cm wooden stick can be put into the box.

stem: Let the lengths of the two right-angled sides and the height of the hypotenuse of the right triangle be $a, b$ and $h$ respectively. Prove: $\frac{1}{a^2} + \frac{1}{b^2} = \frac{1}{h^2}$ .
stem_lead: Let the lengths of the two right-angled sides and the height of the hypotenuse of the right triangle be $a, b$ and $h$ respectively. Prove: $\frac{1}{a^2} + \frac{1}{b^2} = \frac{1}{h^2}$ .

examiner_comment.text:
Let the length of the hypotenuse be \(c\). On the one hand, the area of ​​a right triangle is \(\frac12 ab\), on the other hand, with the hypotenuse as the base and the height as \(h\), we get \(\frac12 ch\), so \(ab=ch\), that is, \(h=\frac{ab}{c}\).
Therefore\(\frac{1}{h^2}=\frac{c^2}{a^2b^2}\). From the Pythagorean theorem\(c^2=a^2+b^2\), we get
\[
\frac{1}{h^2}=\frac{a^2+b^2}{a^2b^2}=\frac{1}{a^2}+\frac{1}{b^2},
\]
The proposition is proved.

mark_scheme.text:
(1) Converse proposition: If the angles of two straight lines are equal, then the two straight lines are parallel. established.
(2) Converse proposition: If the product of two real numbers is a positive number, then both real numbers are positive numbers. Not true (maybe both negative numbers).
(3) Converse proposition: If a triangle is an acute triangle, then it is an equilateral triangle. Not established.
(4) Converse proposition: If the distance from a point in the plane to the two endpoints of a line segment is equal, then this point is on the perpendicular bisector of the line segment. established.

examiner_comment.text:
(1) Use the parallel line determination theorem: the same angles are equal ⇒ the two straight lines are parallel.
(2) If the product is positive, it means that the two numbers have the same sign. They may be both positive or negative, so "both are positive" is not necessarily true.
(3) An acute-angled triangle only requires that the three angles are less than 90°, and it does not necessarily mean that the three sides are equal.
(4) The properties and judgment of the vertical bisector of a line segment are inverse to each other: the distance to both endpoints is equal ⇔ on the vertical bisector.

examiner_comment.text:
From the Pythagorean theorem c=\sqrt{a^2+b^2}. a=2\sqrt{3}+1, b=2\sqrt{3}-1. 
(2\sqrt{3}+1)^2=12+4\sqrt{3}+1=13+4\sqrt{3};
(2\sqrt{3}-1)^2=12-4\sqrt{3}+1=13-4\sqrt{3}. 
The addition gives a^2+b^2=26, so c=\sqrt{26}.

stem: In order to ensure that two straight rails of a railway are parallel to each other, it is only necessary to make the parallel sleepers sandwiched between the rails equal in length. Can you explain why?
stem_lead: In order to ensure that two straight rails of a railway are parallel to each other, it is only necessary to make the parallel sleepers sandwiched between the rails equal in length. Can you explain why?

mark_scheme.text: A sleeper is a transverse line segment connecting two rails and can be seen as the "distance" between two straight lines. If the length of each sleeper is equal, it means that the distance between the two rails is equal everywhere; and in the plane, if the distance between two straight lines is equal everywhere, it is impossible to intersect, so they must be parallel to each other.

examiner_comment.text: Think of the two rails as two straight lines in the same plane, and think of the sleepers as the distance between the two rails measured at different positions. If two straight lines are not parallel, they will intersect. As the position changes, the distance between the two lines will gradually become smaller and be 0 at the intersection. It is impossible to maintain the same distance in multiple places. The lengths of the sleepers in the question are all equal, indicating that the distance between the two rails is the same in many places and remains unchanged, so the two rails should be parallel.

mark_scheme.text: (1) A parallelogram with mutually perpendicular diagonals is a rhombus; (2) A quadrilateral with four equal sides is a rhombus.

examiner_comment.text:
(1) Assume that the diagonals AC and BD of the parallelogram ABCD intersect at point O, and AC⊥BD. The diagonals of a parallelogram bisect each other, so AO=CO and BO=DO. And because AC⊥BD, we get ∠AOB=∠BOC=90°. In the right triangles AOB and COB, OB is a common side, AO=CO, and the included angles are both 90°, so the two triangles are congruent (the two right-angled sides of SAS or right triangles are correspondingly equal), so AB=BC. In the same way, it can be proved that BC=CD or AB=AD. Combining the parallelogram with opposite sides being equal (AB=CD, BC=AD), we can get AB=BC=CD=AD, so ABCD is a rhombus.
(2) Suppose the quadrilateral ABCD satisfies AB=BC=CD=DA. Draw diagonal AC. Then in triangles ABC and ADC: AB=AD, BC=CD, and AC is a common side, so △ABC≌△ADC (SSS), so ∠BAC=∠CAD, ∠BCA=∠ACD. Then AB∥CD, BC∥AD, so ABCD is a parallelogram. And because the two adjacent sides AB=BC, a parallelogram has a set of adjacent sides that are equal, so the four sides are equal, so ABCD is a rhombus.

mark_scheme.text:
(1) is a square. The diagonals of a parallelogram are equal → rectangle; the diagonals are perpendicular to each other → rhombus; it is both a rectangle and a rhombus → square.
(2) is a square. If the diagonals of a rectangle are perpendicular to each other, the rectangle becomes a rhombus; the rectangle is also a rhombus → square.
(3) is a square. The diagonals of a rhombus are equal → the rhombus becomes a rectangle; the rectangle is also a rhombus → a square.
(4) is a square. The diagonals bisect each other perpendicularly → the quadrilateral is a rhombus; and the diagonals are equal → it is also a rectangle; therefore it is a square.

examiner_comment.text:
Key properties:
1) The diagonals of a parallelogram are equal ⇔ a rectangle; the diagonals of a parallelogram are perpendicular to each other ⇔ a rhombus.
2) The diagonals of a rhombus are perpendicular to each other and bisect each other; the diagonals of a rhombus are equal ⇔ square (equivalent to "a rhombus and a rectangle").
Based on this, judge one by one:
(1) Parallelogram + equal diagonals ⇒ rectangle; and perpendicular diagonals ⇒ rhombus; both ⇒ square.
(2) A rectangle is originally a parallelogram, and its diagonals are perpendicular to a rhombus; a rectangle ∩ rhombus ⇒ a square.
(3) Rhombus + diagonals are equal ⇒ rectangle; rhombus ∩ rectangle ⇒ square.
(4) The diagonals are perpendicular to each other and bisect each other ⇒ rhombus; plus the diagonals are equal ⇒ rectangle; therefore it is a square.
